_why: Milestone 0.4. rule-diff.sh reports every per-rule count change between the
last release and this build. Reporting is not accountability: a drop and a
correct narrowing look identical in that output, and the only thing telling
them apart was whoever happened to read the job summary.
This file is the other half. Every rule whose count DROPS must have an entry
here saying why. An unexplained drop fails the job; so does an entry that no
longer describes a real drop, because a ledger nothing validates rots into
The baseline is the last released nox, so entries accumulate between releases
and are cleared when one is cut. `nox_release` records which release they are
written against: if it does not match the tag rule-diff resolved, the ledger
is stale as a whole and says so rather than silently passing.

classifications.duplicate-retired: a second rule reported the same condition; one ID was retired into the other, which carries the alias
classifications.applicability-narrowed: the rule does not apply to this subject or resource kind, and now says so
classifications.sanitizer-recognized: the value reaching the sink is neutralized for this vulnerability class
classifications.refined-away: a cheaper semantic fact refutes the candidate the pattern generated
classifications.rule-removed: the rule was deleted outright; no survivor reports the condition
classifications.context-narrowed: the rule's context requirement is now measured in characters as well as lines, so a keyword far away on the same physical line no longer qualifies as context

entries.reason: SEC-696's pattern is `[a-zA-Z0-9]{32}` with the keyword "timber", and its context requirement was measured in LINES (±4). reitit's dev-resources/json/json100k.json is minified JSON: one line of 101,941 characters. It contains the string "2114 timber wolf trail" — a fake street address in generated test data — and being on the same physical line as everything else in the file, that one word authorised the rule for every 32-character run on it: 421 HIGH-severity findings from one line of fixture JSON. Proximity is now bounded at 512 characters, which is generous for `timber_api_key = "..."` and three orders of magnitude short of a blob. The 3 remaining findings are matches that really do sit near the keyword. No corpus lost an expectation: all 20 precision corpora and the refutation suite are unchanged at 231/0/0 and 37/0/0, and the four real-repo taint controls (ring, certbot, shelljs, plug) are unchanged. A SECOND, later drop takes the remaining 3 (#638). All of them are in the same file: one md5 value, the first 32 characters of a sha256, and the second 32 characters of the same sha256 — digests in generated test data, not Timber API keys. The digest-label refutation added for SEC-163 covers them, including the second half, because the label belongs to the whole hex run and a window a matcher cut out of it inherits `"sha256":`. Every line was read. SEC-696 now has no finding anywhere in the corpus, so the gate witnesses it in neither direction and its behaviour rests on the analyzer tests alone. The rule is now retired outright into SEC-005 (#641), and the measurement that decided it is sharper than the count. On the shape SEC-696 exists for — `timber_api_key = "<32 alphanumerics>"` — it never reached the output at all: SEC-005 wins the dedup contest and reports it. On the shape it gets wrong — a 32-character run anywhere near the word "timber" in prose — it was the ONLY rule that fired. Suppressed exactly where it was right and the sole reporter exactly where it was wrong is not a threshold needing tuning; it is a rule with no unique correct output. It was one of 69 imported from Gitleaks with the shape `[a-zA-Z0-9]{32}` plus one vendor keyword, and the only one of the 69 whose keyword is an ordinary English word AND which carries no secret-shape post-filter. SEC-005 holds the alias with the frozen pattern.

The Serverless Framework family scoped itself with `*.yml`/`*.yaml` alongside the specific names, which made the specific names decoration: every rule in the family applied to every YAML file in any repository. Applicability is now decided by the document — a Serverless rule fires only where the document declares `service`/`provider` — so the filename is a hint about what to parse rather than evidence that the rule applies. Every dropped finding was read: 2 findings on ECS/*/clusters/private-vpc.yaml in aws-cloudformation-templates — CloudFormation templates, not Serverless manifests. No affected file went from flagged to clean: the Kubernetes Secret manifests keep SEC-254/IAC-351/IAC-356 and chronos's workflow keeps IAC-013/IAC-309/SEC-073, so what was removed is the wrong framework's rule reporting on a smell that the right rules still report.

The Kustomize family scoped itself with `*.yaml`/`*.yml` alongside kustomization.yaml, which made the specific names decoration: every rule in the family applied to every YAML file in any repository — the identical shape fixed for the Serverless family in #636. Applicability is now decided by the document: a Kustomize rule fires only where the document declares `kind: Kustomization`, a kustomize.config.k8s.io apiVersion, a kustomization-only field, or a `resources:` LIST (as against the `resources:` MAPPING a Helm values file or a pod spec declares). Measured across the whole corpus, 37 of the family's 40 findings were on documents that are not kustomizations; the 3 that are — IAC-242 on podinfo's dev/staging/production overlays — are unchanged. Every dropped finding was read: 5 across two repositories. 3 on Kubernetes manifests in kubernetes/examples (mysql-pod.yaml, and minio's statefulset and deployment) and 2 on chronos's test/integration/docker-compose.yml. None is a kustomization. The Kubernetes smell is not lost: IAC-031 ("Container image uses latest tag in Kubernetes manifest") now reports all 3 at exactly the same lines — it could not before, because it was anchored with `$` and no `(?m)` and so fired only on a file's last line, fixed in the preceding commit. One file went from flagged to clean: chronos's test/integration/docker-compose.yml, whose only two findings were this rule on `image: ${CHRONOS_IMAGE:-ghcr.io/...:latest}`. No rule covers a latest tag in a compose file, and that gap is real, but a Kustomize rule firing on a docker-compose service was never its answer. Adding geerlingguy/ansible-for-devops to the corpus witnesses 5 more, all read: `image: data:latest`, `flask:latest`, `db:latest` and `test:latest` in Ansible docker_container tasks, plus `${MOLECULE_DISTRO:-rockylinux9}-ansible:latest` in a molecule config. IAC-031 picks up the first four at exactly the same lines. The fifth is not covered by anything: no rule resolves a `${VAR:-default}` substitution before reading the tag, and that gap is named here rather than left to the Kustomize rule. The docker-compose gap named above is now closed by IAC-501 (#642), which resolves `${VAR:-default}` the way Compose does before reading the tag: both chronos findings are reported again, at the same lines, by a rule that says "Docker Compose service … is not pinned" and names the reference the default resolves to. The `${MOLECULE_DISTRO:-rockylinux9}-ansible:latest` form in ansible-for-devops is a molecule config rather than a Compose file and stays unreported.

SEC-163 is "High-entropy hex string detected (possible secret key)", gated by a secret-suggestive keyword anywhere on the line. Measured across the whole corpus it produced 122 findings and every one was read. 117 were the value of a JSON field named `md5` in two generated fixtures in metosin/reitit — `"password":"buffy","salt":"UKfGRyKe","md5":"ff252d31f9d6a7e19f2b28521aa1f367"` — where the sibling `password` field 40 characters away is what authorised them, so the character bound #633 gave SEC-696 would not have removed a single one: the rule was not misjudging distance, it was reporting a password HASH as a possible key. 4 were the gist id in `https://gist.github.com/matthewberryman/fa21ca796c3a2e0dfe8224934b7b055c`, inside a bash script folded into one CloudFormation Fn::Sub scalar. Two refutations now name those cases: a hex value whose own label declares it a digest (md5, sha*, checksum, etag, integrity, …) is a digest, and a hex run in a URL PATH is how that URL names a resource. Both are gated on the value being entirely hexadecimal, so no provider rule can reach them, and the URL check stops at the authority so a credential in userinfo is untouched. The 1 surviving finding is certbot's `challenges.DNS01(token=b"17817c66b60ce2e4012dfad92657527a")`, which the label says is a token. Raising the entropy threshold was tried FIRST and refuted by measurement: require_context also grants the -0.5 context discount, so SEC-163's declared 3.5 runs at 3.0, but charging the declared value removed three real Ceph admin keys from kubernetes/examples through SEC-162, the sibling rule on the same matcher. Recall is controlled by new fixtures — the rule had no true-positive expectation anywhere in 19 precision suites — covering the Python, bytes-literal, JSON and HTTP-header idioms. No file went from flagged to clean and no other rule moved; all 19 precision suites and the refutation suite are unchanged. One number needs reconciling with the job summary above it: the 122 is measured against the CURRENT tree, which already carries #633, while this gate's baseline is v1.35.0 and shows reitit at 12 -> 0. Both are right and they are the same event. At release time SEC-696 was firing on those spans and outranking SEC-163 in dedupBySpecificity (secret_shape beats entropy), so it suppressed 105 of them; #633 took SEC-696 from 421 to 3 on that file and handed the spans to the rule below it, which is why SEC-163 rose 12 -> 117 in the interval. That rise was printed by this gate and never questioned, because rises are reported and only drops are gated. The last 1 goes with the rule itself (#641). SEC-163 is retired into SEC-161, which now carries `hex` as a candidate kind under its own threshold and context requirement. It could not simply be deleted into SEC-161's 5.0, because a threshold is meaningful only against its alphabet — Shannon entropy cannot exceed log2(16) = 4.0 bits over hex, so 5.0 rejects every hex string that exists, which is the defect #467 fixed when the rule shipped at 4.5. The entropy matcher therefore learned to hold a policy per kind first. The one surviving finding, certbot/src/certbot/tests/acme_util.py:19 col 34, is reported by SEC-161 at exactly the same position: SEC-161 goes 21 -> 22 in the same repository and nothing else in the corpus moves. SEC-161 carries the alias with SEC-163's frozen `[0-9a-fA-F]{32,}` pattern, and the `scan.secrets.hex_threshold` / `require_context` settings are unchanged for users — they now write SEC-161's per-kind keys, so raising the generic threshold cannot silently push the hex one past its ceiling.

IAC-243 is "Kustomize uses deprecated vars feature", pattern `vars:\s*\n`, scoped by the family's `*.yaml`/`*.yml` catch-all. An Ansible playbook opens a `vars:` block as a matter of course, so the rule reported 23 of them across geerlingguy/ansible-for-devops -- every `vars:` in every playbook and every test -- as a deprecated Kustomize feature. The document-kind gate added in #637 removes them: none of these files declares `kind: Kustomization`, a kustomize.config.k8s.io apiVersion, a kustomization-only field or a `resources:` list. Every dropped line was read; all 23 are the literal token `vars:` opening an Ansible variable block. This drop appears only now because the repo that witnesses it was added in the same change -- no other entry in the corpus contains an Ansible playbook, which is the reason it was added. 11 files went from flagged to clean (collection/main.yml, jenkins/provision.yml, nodejs-role/playbook.yml, test-plugin/main.yml and 7 under tests/); in each the only finding was this one, and none of them is a kustomization.

IAC-214 ("Ansible collection without version pin") and IAC-211 ("Ansible Galaxy role without version pin") report one condition split by spelling: a Galaxy requirements entry names its dependency with `src:` OR with `name:`, never both, so each rule was blind to half of the condition. IAC-211 now accepts either and carries the IAC-214 alias with the pattern that rule held at retirement, so a waiver written against IAC-214 keeps matching exactly what it used to cover. Every dropped line was read: 13 in geerlingguy/ansible-for-devops, and 12 of them are reported by IAC-211 at exactly the same line — `- name: geerlingguy.apache`, `- name: community.kubernetes` and ten more, all unpinned entries in a requirements.yml. The 13th, https-self-signed/provisioning/vars/main.yml:19, is `server_hostname: https.test`: the last line of a vars file, matched only because `$` meant end of TEXT and the hostname happens to look like a dotted Galaxy name. That is a false positive and it is gone; the file is the one that went from flagged to clean. IAC-211 rises 0 -> 65 in the same repository, every one an unpinned Galaxy requirement in a requirements.yml — it could not fire at all before, being anchored to end of text.

IAC-351 ("CI variable with hardcoded secret", CRITICAL) is a ci-cd rule scoped by ciFilePatterns = {".gitlab-ci.yml", "*.yml", "*.yaml"} — the shape #636 removed from the Serverless family, where the catch-all makes the specific name decoration. Applicability is now decided by the document: a CI rule fires only where the document is a GitHub Actions workflow or a GitLab pipeline. Every dropped finding was read: 8 across two repositories, 2 on Kubernetes Secret manifests in kubernetes/examples (quobyte-admin-secret.yaml, scaleio/secret.yaml) and 6 in Ansible playbooks and task files in ansible-for-devops. None is a CI pipeline. Nothing is lost: IAC-225 ("Hardcoded password in a YAML configuration value") reports all 8 at exactly the same line, which is the right name for the condition — a base64 password in a Kubernetes Secret is not a CI variable. No file went from flagged to clean.

IAC-307 ("GHA workflow targets production environment") is a github-actions rule scoped by ghaFilePatterns = {".github/workflows/*.yml", ".github/workflows/*.yaml", "*.yml", "*.yaml"} — again the catch-all making the specific path decoration. A GitHub Actions rule now fires only where the document declares a top-level `jobs:` with steps in it. The single dropped finding was read: podinfo's deploy/overlays/production/labels.yaml:6, a Kustomize LabelTransformer whose `app.kubernetes.io/environment: production` label the rule read as a workflow environment. That file goes from flagged to clean, correctly: it is a label transformer and the finding was its only one.

IAC-185 shipped as "Helm values or template uses Always image pull policy WITHOUT PINNED TAG" with a pattern that never looked at a tag — it matched `imagePullPolicy: Always` and nothing else. Every dropped finding was read: 3 in kubernetes/examples, and ALL THREE are pinned — `gcr.io/google-samples/cassandra:v14`, `quay.io/pires/hazelcast-kubernetes:3.8_1` and `registry.k8s.io/example-dns-frontend:v1` — so the rule was wrong by its own description on everything it reported. It also called all three "Helm values or template" while every one is a plain Kubernetes manifest, which is the wrong-family naming #636/#637/#644 exist to remove. Always is frequently the RIGHT setting: against a pinned digest it is harmless, and on a mutable tag it is what makes a rollout pick up a changed image. The finding is the PAIR, so the rule now parses the document and reports a container only where an Always policy meets a reference that can change — reusing the reference parser written for IAC-501, which resolves digests, tags and registry ports. The ID is kept, so baselines, VEX statements and nox:ignore comments written against IAC-185 go on resolving. No file went from flagged to clean. The corpus contains no Always-on-unpinned pair, so the rule is now unwitnessed by this gate and rests on its fixtures: five containers across a Deployment, a Pod and a StatefulSet, two reported and three not.

A Dockerfile build-stage reference is not a base image. certbot/tools/docker/Dockerfile:54 reads `FROM certbot AS certbot-plugin`, and `certbot` is a BUILD STAGE declared on line 2 (`FROM python:3.14-alpine3.23 AS certbot`), not an image anyone publishes. ParseDockerfile skipped `scratch` and `${VAR}` references but tracked no stage names, so it emitted the stage as a container component called "certbot" at version "latest" — a dependency the project does not have, in the CycloneDX and SPDX documents downstream consumers trust, and a name handed to OSV where it can match an advisory for an unrelated image. The finding was the visible half of that; the SBOM was the serious half. The parser now records each `AS <name>` before deciding about the image, and dockerfileFromLines shares the same skip predicate rather than copying it: the two walks are index-aligned, so a skip in one and not the other would attach every later finding to the wrong line. Every dropped line was read: 1, the line above. certbot's other 2 CONT-001 findings are real images and are unchanged. A second, later drop (#650): CONT-001 and CONT-002 are now DISJOINT. "Not pinned to a digest" is true of everything "uses latest or no tag" is true of, so every CONT-002 finding was also a CONT-001 finding and `FROM ubuntu` reported one line twice — the second report adding nothing an operator could act on that the first did not say more urgently. Both propositions are real and they are different advice: `FROM ubuntu:22.04` is pinned to a version that can still be re-pushed (CONT-001), `FROM ubuntu` is pinned to nothing at all (CONT-002). CONT-001 now excludes the latest case. Every dropped line was read: 6, all of them untagged images (`FROM busybox`, `FROM nginx`, `FROM centos`, `FROM geerlingguy/docker-ubuntu2004-ansible`), and CONT-002 reports each at the same line. No file went from flagged to clean.

A Dockerfile build-stage reference is not a base image, and it does not use the `latest` tag — it has no tag because it is not an image. certbot/tools/docker/Dockerfile:54 reads `FROM certbot AS certbot-plugin`, and `certbot` is a BUILD STAGE declared on line 2 (`FROM python:3.14-alpine3.23 AS certbot`), not an image anyone publishes. ParseDockerfile skipped `scratch` and `${VAR}` references but tracked no stage names, so it emitted the stage as a container component called "certbot" at version "latest" — a dependency the project does not have, in the CycloneDX and SPDX documents downstream consumers trust, and a name handed to OSV where it can match an advisory for an unrelated image. The finding was the visible half of that; the SBOM was the serious half. The parser now records each `AS <name>` before deciding about the image, and dockerfileFromLines shares the same skip predicate rather than copying it: the two walks are index-aligned, so a skip in one and not the other would attach every later finding to the wrong line. Every dropped line was read: 1, the same line.

`FROM scratch` names Docker's EMPTY pseudo-image: no registry, no tag, no digest. "Unpinned" is not a thing it can be and "pin it" is not advice anyone can take. Every dropped line was read: 2, both the literal line `FROM scratch`, in kubernetes/examples' _archived/explorer/Dockerfile and web/guestbook-go/Dockerfile. Neither file went from flagged to clean. The exclusion was found by comparing IAC-002 with CONT-002, which report the same condition from two analyzers: each had a false positive the other did not — this one, and a build-stage reference — and neither guard could see the other, because the duplicate-rule test compares IaC rules only. The rule is now RETIRED into CONT-002 (#650). Container base-image semantics belong to the analyzer that PARSES the Dockerfile — which is what lets it know `scratch` is not an image, that `FROM certbot` may name a build stage, and what the SBOM component is — rather than to a regex over the FROM line; isDockerfile covers exactly IAC-002's {Dockerfile, Dockerfile.*, *.dockerfile}, so no file scope is lost. All 6 remaining findings were read and CONT-002 reports every one at the same line, carrying the IAC-002 alias so baselines, VEX statements and nox:ignore comments keep resolving. That alias is new machinery: attaching one used to happen only inside rules.Engine.ScanFile, so a finding an analyzer BUILDS by hand — as deps builds CONT-002 — could never have carried it, and this retirement would have silently un-waived every accepted IAC-002. core.attachRetiredIdentities now does it once, centrally, over every analyzer's output.

All 4 dropped findings are lines of base64 inside certbot's integration-test PEM assets (certbot-ci/.../archive/{a,b}.encryption-example.com/{chain1,fullchain1}.pem). SEC-533 is gated on the keyword `ibm`, and the string `iBm` occurs by coincidence inside the certificate's own base64 — so a test certificate was being reported as an IBM API key. The keyword pre-filter matched a vendor keyword as a plain SUBSTRING, so the only evidence a bare-token rule has could be manufactured by coincidence. contextHasKeyword now requires the keyword to appear as a token: a boundary is "not a letter or digit", so `_`, `-` and `.` still separate (posthog matches posthog_api_key), and a keyword carrying a separator is treated as a structured prefix with no right boundary demanded (ghp_, key-, and sk-ant-api, which runs straight into the digits of sk-ant-api03). ExcludeContextKeywords deliberately keep substring matching: a veto that fires too readily suppresses a finding, which is the direction that cannot invent evidence. No coverage is lost: those files are still reported by SEC-004 ("Private key header detected") and SEC-299, which encode the actual proposition — a private key header — rather than a vendor name that happened to appear in the payload. Measured on the pinned fire-rate corpus SEC-533 produced 448 findings, largely this shape, including the Cloudflare cookie value `...Fszr_Msw0B1.IBMki`.

Both dropped findings are lines of base64 inside certbot's integration-test private keys (certbot-ci/.../a.encryption-example.com/privkey1.pem and sample-config/keys/0002_key-certbot.pem). SEC-616 is gated on `fcm`, and `fcm`/`FCM` occurs by coincidence inside the key's own base64, so a test private key was reported as a Firebase Cloud Messaging key. The keyword pre-filter matched a vendor keyword as a plain SUBSTRING, so the only evidence a bare-token rule has could be manufactured by coincidence. contextHasKeyword now requires the keyword to appear as a token: a boundary is "not a letter or digit", so `_`, `-` and `.` still separate (posthog matches posthog_api_key), and a keyword carrying a separator is treated as a structured prefix with no right boundary demanded (ghp_, key-, and sk-ant-api, which runs straight into the digits of sk-ant-api03). ExcludeContextKeywords deliberately keep substring matching: a veto that fires too readily suppresses a finding, which is the direction that cannot invent evidence. No coverage is lost: both files are still reported by SEC-004 and SEC-299, the correct rule for a PEM private key. SEC-616 was the largest single contributor to the 2026-Q2 benchmark at 1,002,602 findings, all of the same shape.

DATA-001 reports PII hard-coded in source and advises "remove or externalize PII data". For an address a project publishes as its own contact point, that advice is wrong and the finding describes no data-handling failure. Two structural exclusions, neither a judgement call: an address inside a `mailto:` URI exists so a reader can write to it, and an address in a package manifest's author/maintainer/contact field is published to the registry with the package. The single dropped finding is chronos docs/index.html:265, `Design partners` — a contact link on a documentation page. Measured on the pinned fire-rate corpus DATA-001 produced 969 findings over just 177 distinct addresses, 716 of them support@crewai.com: 42.9% inside a mailto: URI, 23.6% in a manifest author field, the rest OpenAPI `contact:` blocks and documentation support sections including translated copies of one page. None was a leak. Recall is unchanged for an address sitting where it was not meant to be published — guarded by TestARealAddressInCodeIsStillReported — and the manifest exclusion is scoped to contact fields rather than to the whole file (TestANonContactFieldInAManifestStillReports). Documentation prose and OpenAPI contact blocks are deliberately NOT excluded: both are also published, but recognising them needs block context, and whether nox should report e-mail in docs at all is a question about the rule's purpose rather than its evidence.

DATA-003's pattern describes the SHAPE of a payment card — an issuer prefix and a length — and nothing more. What makes a digit run a card is the Luhn checksum, which every issued card satisfies and a random run satisfies about one time in ten. isPaymentCardNumber now applies it. The single dropped finding is plug lib/plug/conn.ex:1500, the URL `https://www.chromestatus.com/feature/4981025180483584` — a Chrome feature id, 16 digits beginning with 4, reported at HIGH severity as a Visa card. It fails Luhn. A second filter was needed alongside it: measured on the pinned fire-rate corpus DATA-003 produced 560 findings and ALL 560 were floating-point numbers in embedding vectors and notebook output, such as `Similarity: 0.6522269248962402`. The pattern is anchored with `\b` and `.` is not a word character, so the digits after a decimal point are word-bounded. Luhn removes 90.7% of those; the 52 that pass it by chance are still floats, so dropDigitsInsideDecimals removes a match whose preceding byte is a `.` following a digit. Neither half is a heuristic — a real card is written "4111111111111111", never 0.4111111111111111 — and recall on the four card networks' published test numbers is guarded by TestRealCardNumbersAreReported.

SEC-457 ('Detected Iterable API Key', pattern `[a-z0-9]{32}`, keyword 'iterable') matched git commit SHAs in anthropic-sdk-python's CHANGELOG.md because the word 'iterables' appeared elsewhere on the same physical LINE -- up to 180 characters away, separated by a markdown issue link. All 11 dropped findings are in CHANGELOG.md and every one is the commit SHA in a release-note bullet; none is an Iterable credential. Verified by fixture rather than inferred: the same bullet with the SHA adjacent to the keyword still fires in the candidate build, and only the long real line (227 chars) stops, so recall for a genuine key near its vendor word is unchanged.

SEC-659 ('Detected Split API Key') matched the multipart MIME boundary `b"--6b7ba517decee4a450543ea6ae821c82"` in tests/test_client.py, twice, because `.split(b"\r\n")` sat on the PRECEDING line and supplied the 'split' keyword. Both dropped findings are that boundary inside a form-encoding assertion; neither is a Split.io key. Verified by fixture: the four-line excerpt alone reproduces base=1, candidate=0.

SEC-697 ('Detected Literal API Key', pattern `\b[a-zA-Z0-9]{32}\b`) is retired into SEC-005, which carries the alias. Its five findings in anthropic-sdk-python were Python type names that happen to be exactly 32 characters -- `BetaToolComputerUse20241022Param` and `ToolSearchToolRegex20251119Param`, in `__all__` and class declarations -- matched on length alone with no vendor evidence of any kind.

SLOP-001 went 9 -> 4 on anthropic-sdk-python once the analyzer reads lockfiles for TRANSITIVE dependencies. The five dropped imports are `pydantic_core` (x3), `tomli` and `http_snapshot`; all three are declared in requirements-dev.lock under their PEP 503 normalised names (`pydantic-core`, `tomli`, `http-snapshot`), which is why the underscore import form read as undeclared. The four survivors are all `google`, a namespace package genuinely absent from every manifest, so the recall direction is intact: the rule still reports an import nothing declares.
